commentary.hc2:
Headline CPI ran at 3.71% YoY in August 2026, well above the 2.76% core reading, with the gap almost entirely explained by energy. Energy overall surged 16.84% YoY and 2.10% MoM, led by electricity (+30.70% YoY, +6.77% MoM) and gasoline (+27.41% YoY, +3.90% MoM), making those components the dominant upward distortion to headline. Core inflation, by contrast, showed more moderate pressure: shelter contributed at +3.44% YoY, motor vehicle maintenance & repair remained elevated at +7.77% YoY, but new vehicles were nearly flat (+0.57% YoY) and used vehicles and motor vehicle insurance both declined on a year-over-year basis.

• Tire industry: Elevated energy and electricity costs raise both raw-material processing and manufacturing overhead expenses, while the concurrent softness in new and used vehicle prices signals restrained consumer vehicle acquisition—a combination that pressures margin on replacement tires and may dampen OE fitment volumes simultaneously.
commentary.mfg2:
Electricity costs rose sharply at 30.70% year-over-year, far outpacing the other components. Natural gas posted a modest gain of 3.81%, while food at home and household furnishings increased at comparatively low rates of 2.65% and 2.27%, respectively. The spread between the highest and lowest components exceeds 28 percentage points, indicating heavily uneven inflation pressure across this basket.

• Tire industry: Electricity's 30.70% surge directly pressures energy-intensive tire manufacturing operations—including mixing, curing, and vulcanization processes—where power costs represent a significant share of production overhead.
commentary.transp2:
Gasoline prices rose 27.41% year-over-year in August 2026, while fuel oil increased only marginally at 0.39%. Airline fares posted the sharpest gain among the components at 28.91%, and motor vehicle insurance was the sole component to decline, falling 5.10%.

• Tire industry: The 27.41% surge in gasoline costs raises fleet operators' total cost-per-mile, increasing pressure on vehicle utilization efficiency and potentially accelerating demand for fuel-efficient tire specifications to offset operating expenses.
commentary.fed2:
Headline CPI at 3.71% year-over-year sits 171 basis points above the Fed's 2% symmetric target, and the 0.40% monthly print annualizes to roughly 4.9%, indicating that near-term momentum has not decelerated to target-consistent levels. Core at 2.76% year-over-year suggests underlying price pressure remains elevated even after stripping out food and energy, leaving the gap to target at 76 basis points on that measure. Both readings are consistent with a data environment in which the Fed has limited basis to declare disinflation complete, keeping the conditions for rate cuts more distant than they would be if either measure were at or below 2%.

• Tire industry: Sustained above-target inflation and the associated higher-for-longer rate environment raises borrowing costs on capital-intensive inventory and fleet-financing programs, while persistent input-cost pressures in petrochemical feedstocks—themselves correlated with elevated general price levels—compress manufacturer margins unless offset
commentary.lens2:
Headline CPI ran at 3.71% YoY in August 2026, well above the core reading of 2.76%, with the gap driven almost entirely by energy. Gasoline (+27.41% YoY, +3.90% MoM) and electricity (+30.70% YoY, +6.77% MoM) account for the bulk of the overshoot above core. Airline fares (+28.91% YoY) add a second transport-adjacent surge, likely partly reflecting fuel pass-through. Shelter continues to contribute steadily at +3.44% YoY but is not accelerating sharply on a monthly basis (+0.26% MoM). Motor vehicle maintenance & repair (+7.77% YoY, +1.08% MoM) remains elevated, while new vehicle prices are nearly flat (+0.57% YoY) and used vehicles are in outright deflation (-2.32% YoY). Motor vehicle insurance is also deflating (-5.10% YoY), unwinding prior-cycle increases. Food pressure is modest and decelerating, with food at home up only 0.04% MoM.

commentary.tire2:
**Auto & Tire CPI Channel — August 2026 (Year-over-Year)**

• New vehicle prices posted marginal inflation of +0.57%, while used vehicle prices contracted 2.32%, indicating continued normalization in the secondary market and reduced pricing power across the vehicle transaction segment.

• Motor vehicle maintenance & repair costs surged 7.77% year-over-year, the sharpest move in the channel, reflecting elevated labor rates and parts costs at the service level; motor vehicle insurance fell 5.10%, suggesting insurers are recalibrating premiums following prior-cycle rate increases, potentially compressing claims-driven repair demand at the margin.

• The divergence between a cooling vehicle purchase market and accelerating maintenance costs points to a consumer base holding existing vehicles longer, driving higher service frequency and parts consumption rather than new purchase activity.

---

• Tire industry: The combination of flat new-vehicle sales inflation and a 7.77% surge in maintenance & repair CPI signals a fleet-aging dynamic in which consumers are deferring vehicle replacement, directly expanding the replacement tire market segment and supporting volume demand for tires sold through the service and independent retail channel rather than OEM fitment.

commentary.ppilens2:
Synthetic rubber producer prices rose 8.35% year-over-year in August 2026, running well above the broader rubber and plastic products index, which advanced 5.58% over the same period. Finished passenger car tire prices increased 2.61% year-over-year on a not-seasonally-adjusted basis, while the wider tires and tubes category rose 1.72% YoY—both trailing upstream input inflation by a substantial margin.

• Synthetic rubber (NSA) posted +8.35% YoY in August 2026, the fastest-moving component in the stack and the primary upstream cost driver.
• Rubber & plastic products (NSA) advanced +5.58% YoY, confirming broad-based upstream pressure across the elastomer and polymer input complex.
• Finished tire prices (NSA) lagged upstream costs materially: passenger car tires +2.61% YoY and tires & tubes +1.72% YoY, indicating a spread of roughly 560–665 basis points between synthetic rubber input inflation and downstream finished-goods price recovery.

• Tire industry: The 660-basis-point gap between synthetic rubber input cost inflation (+8.35%) and finished passenger car tire pricing (+2.61%) signals that manufacturers are absorbing a significant portion of upstream cost increases rather than passing them through fully at the finished-goods level.
